tlp.title: 🚦 🚦 🚦 🚦 🚦 🚦 Traffic Light Protocol 2.0
tlp.description: The Traffic Light Protocol - or short: TLP - was designed with the objective to create a favorable classification scheme for sharing sensitive information while keeping the control over its distribution at the same time.
markdownEnumDescriptions:
### ⚪ clear

🔑 **Identifier** : `TLP:CLEAR`

_Vocabulary_ : `Traffic Light Protocol`

 





---

Recipients can spread this to the world, there is no limit on disclosure.

### 🟢 green

🔑 **Identifier** : `TLP:GREEN`

_Vocabulary_ : `Traffic Light Protocol`

 





---

Limited disclosure, recipients can spread this within their community. Sources may use TLP:GREEN when information is useful to increase awareness within their wider community.

### 🟠 amber

🔑 **Identifier** : `TLP:AMBER`

_Vocabulary_ : `Traffic Light Protocol`

 





---

Limited disclosure, recipients can only spread this on a need-to-know basis within their organization and its clients.

### 🟠 amber+strict

🔑 **Identifier** : `TLP:AMBER+STRICT`

_Vocabulary_ : `Traffic Light Protocol`

 





---

Similar to TLP:AMBER, but restricts sharing to the organization only.

### 🔴 red

🔑 **Identifier** : `TLP:RED`

_Vocabulary_ : `Traffic Light Protocol`

 





---

For the eyes and ears of individual recipients only, no further disclosure.

classification.title: 💡 💡 💡 💡 💡 💡 Data Classification
markdownEnumDescriptions:
### 💡 RESTREINT UE/EU RESTRICTED

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0001`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



💶 **European Union Classified Information** : _In order for the Council to be able to work in all areas which require the use of EU classified information (EUCI),
it needs to have a comprehensive security system to protect this information. The Council decision on the security
rules for protecting EU classified information lays down the basic pr..._



---

The unauthorised disclosure of this information could be disadvantageous to the interests of the EU or one or more of the member states.

### 💡 CONFIDENTIEL UE/EU CONFIDENTIAL

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0002`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



💶 **European Union Classified Information** : _In order for the Council to be able to work in all areas which require the use of EU classified information (EUCI),
it needs to have a comprehensive security system to protect this information. The Council decision on the security
rules for protecting EU classified information lays down the basic pr..._



---

The unauthorised disclosure of this information could cause exceptionally grave prejudice to the essential interests of the EU or one or more of the member states.

### 💡 SECRET UE/EU SECRET

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0003`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



💶 **European Union Classified Information** : _In order for the Council to be able to work in all areas which require the use of EU classified information (EUCI),
it needs to have a comprehensive security system to protect this information. The Council decision on the security
rules for protecting EU classified information lays down the basic pr..._



---

The unauthorised disclosure of this information could seriously harm the essential interests of the EU or one or more of the member states.

### 💡 TRÈS SECRET UE/EU TOP SECRET

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0004`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



💶 **European Union Classified Information** : _In order for the Council to be able to work in all areas which require the use of EU classified information (EUCI),
it needs to have a comprehensive security system to protect this information. The Council decision on the security
rules for protecting EU classified information lays down the basic pr..._



---

The unauthorised disclosure of this information could cause exceptionally grave prejudice to the essential interests of the EU or one or more of the member states.

### 💡 NATO Unclassified

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0006`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



🪖 **NATO CLASSIFICATION MARKINGS** : _NATO information is information that has been generated by or for NATO, or member nation 
originated-information that has been released into the NATO security system. Information marked 
“NATO” is the property of NATO. NATO classified information contributed by a member nation 
remains the property ..._



---

This is applied to official information that is the property of NATO but 
does not meet the criteria for classification. Access to this information 
by non-NATO entities is permitted when such access would not be 
detrimental to NATO.


### 💡 NATO RESTRICTED

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0007`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



🪖 **NATO CLASSIFICATION MARKINGS** : _NATO information is information that has been generated by or for NATO, or member nation 
originated-information that has been released into the NATO security system. Information marked 
“NATO” is the property of NATO. NATO classified information contributed by a member nation 
remains the property ..._



---

Applied to information whose unauthorized disclosure would be 
disadvantageous to the interests of NATO. Though similar safeguards 
are applied to FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY, OFFICIAL USE ONLY, or 
SENSITIVE, BUT UNCLASSIFIED information, NATO RESTRICTED 
is a security classification.


### 💡 NATO CONFIDENTIAL

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0008`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



🪖 **NATO CLASSIFICATION MARKINGS** : _NATO information is information that has been generated by or for NATO, or member nation 
originated-information that has been released into the NATO security system. Information marked 
“NATO” is the property of NATO. NATO classified information contributed by a member nation 
remains the property ..._



---

Applied to information whose unauthorized disclosure would be 
damaging to NATO interests.


### 💡 NATO CONFIDENTIAL ATOMAL

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0009`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



🪖 **NATO CLASSIFICATION MARKINGS** : _NATO information is information that has been generated by or for NATO, or member nation 
originated-information that has been released into the NATO security system. Information marked 
“NATO” is the property of NATO. NATO classified information contributed by a member nation 
remains the property ..._



---

Applied to information whose unauthorized disclosure would be 
damaging to NATO interests.

This designation is added to the NATO security classification when 
applicable. For example, COSMIC TOP SECRET ATOMAL (CTS-A).
ATOMAL information applies to U.S. RESTRICTED DATA or 
FORMERLY RESTRICTED DATA or United Kingdom Atomic 
Information released to NATO.

🔑 **Identifier** : `DCM0010`

_Vocabulary_ : `Data Classification Marking`

 



🪖 **NATO CLASSIFICATION MARKINGS** : _NATO information is information that has been generated by or for NATO, or member nation

### 🖲️ Control Server

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0100`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Control_Server

---

A device which acts as both a server and controller, that hosts the control software used in communicating with lower-level control devices in an ICS network (e.g. Remote Terminal Units (RTUs) and Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs)).

### 🗄️ Data Historian

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0101`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Engineering_Workstation

---

A centralized database located on a computer installed in the control system DMZ supporting external corporate user data access for archival and analysis using statistical process control and other techniques.

### 👷 Engineering Workstation

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0102`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Engineering_Workstation

---

The engineering workstation is usually a high-end very reliable computing platform designed for configuration, maintenance and diagnostics of the control system applications and other control system equipment. The system is usually made up of redundant hard disk drives, high speed network interface, reliable CPUs, performance graphics hardware, and applications that provide configuration and monitoring tools to perform control system application development, compilation and distribution of system modifications.

### ⌨️ Field Controller/RTU/PLC/IED

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0103`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Field_Controller/RTU/PLC/IED

---

Controller terminology depends on the type of system they are associated with. They provide typical processing capabilities. Controllers, sometimes referred to as Remote Terminal Units (RTU) and Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC), are computerized control units that are typically rack or panel mounted with modular processing and interface cards. The units are collocated with the process equipment and interface through input and output modules to the various sensors and controlled devices. Most utilize a programmable logic-based application that provides scanning and writing of data to and from the IO interface modules and communicates with the control system network via various communications methods, including serial and network communications.

### 🎰 Human-Machine Interface

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0104`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Human-Machine_Interface

---

In computer science and human-computer interaction, the Human-Machine Interface (HMI) refers to the graphical, textual and auditory information the program presents to the user (operator) using computer monitors and audio subsystems, and the control sequences (such as keystrokes with the computer keyboard, movements of the computer mouse, and selections with the touchscreen) the user employs to control the program. Currently the following types of HMI are the most common: 

Graphical user interfaces(GUI) accept input via devices such as computer keyboard and mouse and provide articulated graphical output on the computer monitor. 
Web-based user interfaces accept input and provide output by generating web pages which are transported via the network and viewed by the user using a web browser program. The operations user must be able to control the system and assess the state of the system. Each control system vendor provides a unique look-and-feel to their basic HMI applications. An older, not gender-neutral version of the term is man-machine interface (MMI).
The system may expose several user interfaces to serve different kinds of users. User interface screens may be optimized to provide the appropriate information and control interface to operations users, engineering users and management users.

### 🖲️ Input/Output Server

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0105`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Input/Output_Server

---

The Input/Output (I/O) server provides the interface between the control system LAN applications and the field equipment monitored and controlled by the control system applications. The I/O server, sometimes referred to as a Front-End Processor (FEP) or Data Acquisition Server (DAS), converts the control system application data into packets that are transmitted over various types of communications media to the end device locations. The I/O server also converts data received from the various end devices over different communications mediums into data formatted to communicate with the control system networked applications.

### 🦺 Safety Instrumented System/Protection Relay

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0106`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://collaborate.mitre.org/attackics/index.php/Safety_Instrumented_System/Protection_Relay

---

A safety instrumented system (SIS) takes automated action to keep a plant in a safe state, or to put it into a safe state, when abnormal conditions are present. The SIS may implement a single function or multiple functions to protect against various process hazards in your plant.3 The function of protective relaying is to cause the prompt removal from service of an element of a power system when it suffers a short circuit or when it starts to operate in any abnormal manner that might cause damage or otherwise interfere with the effective operation of the rest of the system.

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0107`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://www.ibm.com/cloud/learn/faas

---

FaaS (Function-as-a-Service) is a type of cloud-computing service that allows you to execute code in response to events without the complex infrastructure typically associated with building and launching microservices applications.

### 🗣️ Business Communication Tools

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0108`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 





---

Enterprise communication consists of an organization's tools and practices to collaborate and share information internally and externally. Common examples include phone, email, instant messaging, and face-to-face video meetings.

### 🧩 Windows API

🔑 **Identifier** : `TGT0109`

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 



https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/apiindex/windows-api-list

---

The Windows API, informally WinAPI, is Microsoft's core set of application programming interfaces (APIs) available in the Microsoft Windows operating systems. The name Windows API collectively refers to several different platform implementations that are often referred to by their own names (for example, Win32 API). Almost all Windows programs interact with the Windows API.

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

 





---

Dedicated network segment containing operational technology assets including PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, and SCADA servers, typically isolated from corporate IT networks.

---

RS-232/RS-485 serial connections used for point-to-point communication between OT devices, often using Modbus RTU or DNP3 protocols.

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

Specialized time-series database for collecting and storing process data from industrial control systems, used for trending, analysis, and regulatory compliance.

_Vocabulary_ : `Targets`

Central system in SCADA architecture that collects data from and sends commands to RTUs and PLCs across geographically distributed sites.

watchlist_alias.title: Watchlist Alias
watchlist_alias.markdownDescription:
Aliases can be used as a more friendly name to consume the watchlist in queries.
By default, the aliases and the watchlist name are the same as the lookup csv file name.

💬 3 to 64 characters long : 

- First character must be a letter
- Last character can be a letter or a number

---

**Updating an existing watchlist alias**

💡 Ensure readiness of existing queries before updating as they use the alias as a reference. 

⚡ When updating the alias of a watchlist, the deployer will only delete the previous
watchlist once the new one with the updated alias was created, leaving no gaps.

regex.expression.description: Regular Expression used when validating the column

list.values.description: Defined list of values that the values in the lookup column must match.

type.title: Data Type
type.description: Describe the expected data format of the column

anyOf.description: Generic validation, everything will pass.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🤷‍♂️ Any type

Generic validation, everything will pass.

⚠️ _This type is not recommended as it bypasses validation, and should only be used
in exceptional scenario where other types won't apply._

💡 Use the `regex` type if you require a custom validation type or contact CoreTIDE Governance.

anyOf.description: Will explicitely check for string, and reject other format that can be converted to a string.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🧵 Strings

Will check for `strings`, and reject other format that
can be converted to a `integer`, `float` or `boolean`.

**✅ Accepted Values**
- NameSurname
- Name Surname
- Word 19 Word 1.234

**❌ Rejected Values**
- 10,230
- 11
- 1.1
- TRUE _Accepted boolean True value, use boolean type instead_

anyOf.description:
Expects an integer with no separators such as "," or "." (12,000,000 is not accepted, use 12000000).
For values with a decimal point, use the float type
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🔢 Integers

Accepts an integer (whole number). 💡For numbers with a decimal point, use the _float_ type.

⚠️ **Thousands separators are not accepted**

⚠️ .0 decimal points are tolerated, as many tools will treat it as an integer. 

- ❌ `19,000,000` is invalid, `19000000` is expected
- ✅ `1.00` is a float, but is tolerated
- ✅ `19` is a valid integer

anyOf.description:
Expects a number with a floating point OR an integer.
If only expecting integer, use the integer type instead.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🛟 Floating point values

Expects a number with a floating point OR an integer.

💡If only expecting integer, use the _integer_ type instead.

⚠️ **Thousands separators are not accepted**

⚠️ `.` is expected as a decimal separator, not `,`

- ❌ `19,000.1` is invalid, `19000.1` is expected
- ❌ `19,6` is invalid, `19.6` is expected
- ✅ `19` is an integer, and also a valid float
- ✅ `19.01` is a valid float

anyOf.description: Accepts a value representing a [true | True | TRUE | 1] or [false | False | FALSE | 0] state.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### ✅ Boolean Values 
Accepts a value represented a true or false state. 

| **✅ Accepted "True" Values** | **❌ Accepted "False" Values** |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| true                          | false                           |
| True                          | False                           |
| TRUE                          | FALSE                           |
| 1                             | 0                               |

anyOf.description: Custom regex validation
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🔎 Regular Expression

Leverage a regular expression to provide a custom validation.

💡 It is strongly suggested to test your regex on a playground such as
[🔗Regex 101](https://regex101.com) and toggle the `Python` Flavor for maximum compatibility.

👉 You will have to enter the regex using the required `regex.expression` keyword

⚠️ CoreTIDE does not vet for any third party site to test regular expression,
we recommend to **not upload any critical data on a third-party controlled site**.

anyOf.description: Check whether the input value belongs to a predefined list
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 📃 Predefined List

👉 You will have to input the required value with `list.values`

⚠️ Leading and trailing whitespaces will be ignored during validation, as the overall data pipeline
will remove them as well

anyOf.description:
Standard email format, such as coretide@tide.com. IP addresses within the email
address are not expected.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 📧 Email Address
Standard email format, such as described in [🔗 RFC 5322](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322)

- ✅ coretide@tide.com
- ✅ tide.governance@tide.babel
- ❌ coretide@10.0.0.19
                
💡 Any Top-Level Domain (`tld`) is accepted, as long as the `user@domain.tld` format is respected.

anyOf.description:
Standard url format, such as http://www.example.com/index.html.
For simple FQDN validation with no URI, use the domain type instead.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🔗 URL Address
Standard URL format, such as described in [🔗 URL Living Standard](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

💡 For simple domain validation with no URI, use the _domain_ instead.

👉 Expects the standard pattern `FQDN/URI`, meaning `[ftp | http | https]://(subdomain.)domain.tld/resource`

anyOf.description:
Standard domain name format, such as (subdomain.)domain@tld.
A full FQDN (containing protocol) is not expected.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🌐 Domain Name

Standard domain name format, such as described in [🔗 RFC 1034](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1034)

💡A full FQDN (containing protocol) is not expected. For full `FQDN` + `URI`, use _url_ instead

👉 Expects the standard pattern `FQDN/URI`, meaning `[ftp | http | https]://(subdomain.)domain.tld/resource`

anyOf.description: IP version 4 format, such as 10.0.0.19
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🌐 IP Address

IPv4 addresses, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | IP Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_address)

💡 For IPv6 validation, use _ip::v6_ instead.

👉 Expects the common 32 bit (4 bytes) decimal format `(0->253).(0->253).(0->253).(0->253)`

### 🌐 IP version 6 Address

IPv6 addresses, such as descripbed in [🔗 Wikipedia | IPv6 Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPv6_address)

👉 Accepts both upper and lower case hexadecimal values, such as
`2001:db8:3333:4444:5555:6666:7777:8888` and `2001:db8:3333:4444:CCCC:DDDD:EEEE:FFFF`

anyOf.description: Universal Unique Identifier as a 128 bit value
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🆔 Universal Unique Identifier

UUIDs such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | Universal Unique Identifider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier)

👉 Accepts any version of UUID, as the only difference is the generation
method and not the format.

anyOf.description: MD5 Hashes
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### #️⃣ MD5 Hash

Valid MD5 Hash values, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | MD5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MD5)

anyOf.description: SHA-1 Hashes
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### #️⃣ Secure Hash Algorithm 1 Hash

Valid SHA-1 Hash values, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | MD5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1)

anyOf.description: SHA-256 Hashes
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### #️⃣ Secure Hash Algorithm 2 [256 bit digest] Hash

Valid SHA256 Hash values, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | SHA-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2)

search_key.title: Watchlist Search Key
search_key.markdownDescription:
Name of a column in your watchlist that you expect to use as a join with
other data or as a frequent object of searches.

---

**Updating an existing watchlist search key**

💡 Ensure readiness of existing queries before updating as they use the search key as a reference. 

⚠️ Changing the search key will result in a deletion and recreation of the watchlist
in a synchroneous manner leaving a small period of time where the lookup won't be complete.

watchlist_alias.title: Watchlist Alias
watchlist_alias.markdownDescription:
Aliases can be used as a more friendly name to consume the watchlist in queries.
By default, the aliases and the watchlist name are the same as the lookup csv file name.

💬 3 to 64 characters long : 

- First character must be a letter
- Last character can be a letter or a number
- Other characters can be letters, numbers, underscores `_` or hyphens `-`

---

**Updating an existing watchlist alias**

💡 Ensure readiness of existing queries before updating as they use the alias as a reference. 

⚡ When updating the alias of a watchlist, the deployer will only delete the previous
watchlist once the new one with the updated alias was created, leaving no gaps.

list.values.description: Defined list of values that the values in the lookup column must match.

type.title: Data Type
type.description: Describe the expected data format of the column

anyOf.description: Generic validation, everything will pass.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🤷‍♂️ Any type

Generic validation, everything will pass.

⚠️ _This type is not recommended as it bypasses validation, and should only be used
in exceptional scenario where other types won't apply._

💡 Use the `regex` type if you require a custom validation type or contact CoreTIDE Governance.

anyOf.description: Will explicitely check for string, and reject other format that can be converted to a string.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🧵 Strings

Will check for `strings`, and reject other format that
can be converted to a `integer`, `float` or `boolean`.

**✅ Accepted Values**
- NameSurname
- Name Surname
- Word 19 Word 1.234

**❌ Rejected Values**
- 10,230
- 11
- 1.1
- TRUE _Accepted boolean True value, use boolean type instead_

anyOf.description:
Expects an integer with no separators such as "," or "." (12,000,000 is not accepted, use 12000000).
For values with a decimal point, use the float type
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🔢 Integers

Accepts an integer (whole number). 💡For numbers with a decimal point, use the _float_ type.

⚠️ **Thousands separators are not accepted**

⚠️ .0 decimal points are tolerated, as many tools will treat it as an integer. 

- ❌ `19,000,000` is invalid, `19000000` is expected
- ✅ `1.00` is a float, but is tolerated
- ✅ `19` is a valid integer

anyOf.description:
Expects a number with a floating point OR an integer.
If only expecting integer, use the integer type instead.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🛟 Floating point values

Expects a number with a floating point OR an integer.

💡If only expecting integer, use the _integer_ type instead.

⚠️ **Thousands separators are not accepted**

⚠️ `.` is expected as a decimal separator, not `,`

- ❌ `19,000.1` is invalid, `19000.1` is expected
- ❌ `19,6` is invalid, `19.6` is expected
- ✅ `19` is an integer, and also a valid float
- ✅ `19.01` is a valid float

anyOf.description: Accepts a value representing a [true | True | TRUE | 1] or [false | False | FALSE | 0] state.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### ✅ Boolean Values 
Accepts a value represented a true or false state. 

| **✅ Accepted "True" Values** | **❌ Accepted "False" Values** |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| true                          | false                           |
| True                          | False                           |
| TRUE                          | FALSE                           |
| 1                             | 0                               |

anyOf.description: Custom regex validation
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🔎 Regular Expression

Leverage a regular expression to provide a custom validation.

💡 It is strongly suggested to test your regex on a playground such as
[🔗Regex 101](https://regex101.com) and toggle the `Python` Flavor for maximum compatibility.

👉 You will have to enter the regex using the required `regex.expression` keyword

⚠️ CoreTIDE does not vet for any third party site to test regular expression,
we recommend to **not upload any critical data on a third-party controlled site**.

anyOf.description: Check whether the input value belongs to a predefined list
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 📃 Predefined List

👉 You will have to input the required value with `list.values`

⚠️ Leading and trailing whitespaces will be ignored during validation, as the overall data pipeline
will remove them as well

anyOf.description:
Standard email format, such as coretide@tide.com. IP addresses within the email
address are not expected.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 📧 Email Address
Standard email format, such as described in [🔗 RFC 5322](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322)

- ✅ coretide@tide.com
- ✅ tide.governance@tide.babel
- ❌ coretide@10.0.0.19
                
💡 Any Top-Level Domain (`tld`) is accepted, as long as the `user@domain.tld` format is respected.

anyOf.description:
Standard url format, such as http://www.example.com/index.html.
For simple FQDN validation with no URI, use the domain type instead.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🔗 URL Address
Standard URL format, such as described in [🔗 URL Living Standard](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/)

💡 For simple domain validation with no URI, use the _domain_ instead.

👉 Expects the standard pattern `FQDN/URI`, meaning `[ftp | http | https]://(subdomain.)domain.tld/resource`

anyOf.description:
Standard domain name format, such as (subdomain.)domain@tld.
A full FQDN (containing protocol) is not expected.
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🌐 Domain Name

Standard domain name format, such as described in [🔗 RFC 1034](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1034)

💡A full FQDN (containing protocol) is not expected. For full `FQDN` + `URI`, use _url_ instead

👉 Expects the standard pattern `FQDN/URI`, meaning `[ftp | http | https]://(subdomain.)domain.tld/resource`

anyOf.description: IP version 4 format, such as 10.0.0.19
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🌐 IP Address

IPv4 addresses, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | IP Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IP_address)

💡 For IPv6 validation, use _ip::v6_ instead.

👉 Expects the common 32 bit (4 bytes) decimal format `(0->253).(0->253).(0->253).(0->253)`

### 🌐 IP version 6 Address

IPv6 addresses, such as descripbed in [🔗 Wikipedia | IPv6 Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPv6_address)

👉 Accepts both upper and lower case hexadecimal values, such as
`2001:db8:3333:4444:5555:6666:7777:8888` and `2001:db8:3333:4444:CCCC:DDDD:EEEE:FFFF`

anyOf.description: Universal Unique Identifier as a 128 bit value
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 🆔 Universal Unique Identifier

UUIDs such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | Universal Unique Identifider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universally_unique_identifier)

👉 Accepts any version of UUID, as the only difference is the generation
method and not the format.

anyOf.description: MD5 Hashes
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### #️⃣ MD5 Hash

Valid MD5 Hash values, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | MD5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MD5)

anyOf.description: SHA-1 Hashes
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### #️⃣ Secure Hash Algorithm 1 Hash

Valid SHA-1 Hash values, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | MD5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1)

anyOf.description: SHA-256 Hashes
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### #️⃣ Secure Hash Algorithm 2 [256 bit digest] Hash

Valid SHA256 Hash values, such as described in [🔗 Wikipedia | SHA-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2)

chaining.title: Vector Chaining
chaining.description: Describe the relation of this threat vector to others
chaining.markdownDescription:
**Describe the relation of this threat vector to others**

💡 The relation is always **from** the vector containing the chain
**to** the vector described in the chain

```yaml
id: TVM1919
...
chaining:
⠀⠀- relation: sequence::succeeds
⠀⠀⠀⠀vector: TVM1234
```

👉 Translates to : _TVM1919 **succeeds** (or _is succeeding_) TVM1234._

schema.title: Schema identifier and version
schema.description: Identifier of the schema at its current version

status.title: Status of the use-case
status.description: Define the status according to use case development life cycle process

contributors.title: Development Contributors
contributors.description: Individuals who supported creating, enriching or tuning the detection.

tenants.title: Target Tenants
tenants.description: Override the default organizations and deploy to selected tenants only.

flags.title: Flags
flags.description: Flags allow to customize the rule behaviour using the modifiers framework

template.title: Template Information
template.description:
Optional metadata about the template this rule was created from. You
can find this information in the Sentinel GUI when viewing template rule.
This will enable tracking of rules created from templates in the Sentinel GUI

uuid.title: UUID of the template rule
uuid.description:
The uuid of the alert rule template used to create this rule.
You can find this information in the Sentinel rule repository (https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/),
or by browsing https://analyticsrules.exchange/

version.title: Template Version
version.description:
The version of the alert rule template used to create
this rule - in format <a.b.c>, where all are numbers,
for example 1.0.2

operator.description:
The operation against the threshold that triggers alert rule.

⚠️ If you create a NRT rule, this value must be removed or commented out (NRT rules trigger an alert on the first match)

threshold.title: Event threshold
threshold.description:
If amount of events is higher than threshold (during the timeframe) the alert is triggered. 

⚠️ If you create a NRT rule, this value must be removed or commented out (NRT rules trigger an alert on the first match)

nrt.title: Near Real Time Rule
nrt.description:
NRT rules are hard-coded to run once every minute and capture events
ingested in the preceding minute, so as to be able to supply you with
information as up-to-the-minute as possible.

⚠️ You can not turn a ScheduledAlert into a NRT Rule or vice versa. Once
the MDR is deployed under this UUID, if it must be transformed into
a different type, a new UUID must be attributed and the previous rule
manually removed from Sentinel.

frequency.title: Recurring Search Interval
frequency.description: Time intervals at which the scheduled search should be ran at, from 5m to up to 14days. Format is X d|h|m. If you create a NRT rule, this value must be removed or commented out.
frequency.markdownDescription:
Time intervals at which the scheduled search should be ran at

💡 _You can use `d`, `h` or `m` to represent `days`, `hours` and `minutes` respectively_

Note that Sentinel supports frequency intervals **from 5 minutes up to 14 days** only, translating to the
maximum values for lookback configuration : `14d`, `337h` or `20160m`

⚠️ If you create a NRT rule, this value must be removed or commented out (NRT rules work on the smallest possible timeframe)

lookback.title: Lookback Configuration
lookback.description: Duration of logs to search in, up to 14 days. Format is X d|h|m. If you create a NRT rule, this value must be removed or commented out.
lookback.markdownDescription:
Duration of logs to search in. 

💡 _You can use `d`, `h` or `m` to represent `days`, `hours` and `minutes` respectively_

Note that Sentinel supports lookback periods **up to 14 days** only, translating to the
maximum values for lookback configuration : `14d`, `337h` or `20160m`

⚠️ If you create a NRT rule, this value must be removed or commented out (NRT rules work on the smallest possible timeframe)

alert.title: Alert Configuration
alert.description: Alert Details allow analytic rules to have dynamic values for the Displayed name, Description, Tactics and Severity properties of the alert. By using dynamic alert details, the same rule can generate different incidents, for example with different severity. Also, the information displayed to the analyst can include variable information such as relevant entity names to  help the analyst understand the incident faster.

create_incident.title: Create Incident
create_incident.description: Create incidents from alerts triggered by this analytics rule

suppression.title: Alert Suppression
suppression.description: The duration to wait since last time this alert rule been triggered. Set to "false" to disable all suppression.

title.title: Alert Display Name Format
title.description: Free text with field names embedded using the format {{columnName}}. Up to 256 chars and 3 placeholders.

description.title: Alert Description Format
description.description: Free text with field names embedded using the format {{columnName}}. Up to 5000 chars and 3 placeholders

severity.title: Alert Severity
severity.description: Severity the alert will be raised with. Overrides MDR Base Severity

techniques.title: MITRE ATT&CK Techniques
techniques.description:
Mapping of relevant tactics - Warning : it's currently not possible
to support all valid techniques as a schema for each target system,
as they all support different variants and version of ATT&CK.
You must check on the GUI what techniques are available and replicate here.

custom_details.title: Custom Details
custom_details.description: Surface particular event parameters and their values in alerts that comprise those events, by adding key-value pairs below.

key.description: Enter a name of your choosing that will appear as the field name in alerts.

entity.title: Sentinel Entity
entity.description: Entity Type for which attributes available as identifier are mapped to.
entity.markdownDescription:
Each mapped entity can identify **_up to ten entities._**

- If an alert contains more than ten items that correspond to a single entity
mapping, only the first ten will be recognized as entities and be able to be analyzed as such.
- This limitation applies to actual mappings, not to entity types. So if you have three
different mapped entities for IP addresses (say, source, destination, and gateway), each of
those mappings can accommodate ten entities.

anyOf.description: User account entity type
anyOf.markdownDescription:
### 👤 Account

_User account entity type_

Required identifiers : _Sid, Name, AadUserId, PUID, ObjectGuid_

**Strong identifiers of an account entity:**

- Name + UPNSuffix
- AadUserId
- Sid + Host (required for SIDs of builtin accounts)
- Sid (except for SIDs of builtin accounts)
- Name + NTDomain (unless NTDomain is a builtin domain, for example "Workgroup")
- Name + Host (if NTDomain is a builtin domain, for example "Workgroup")
- Name + DnsDomain
- PUID
- ObjectGuid

**Weak identifiers of an account entity:**

- Name

Each one of the identifiers in the **required identifiers** column is minimally necessary to identify its entity.
However, a required identifier might not, by itself, be sufficient to provide _unique_ identification.
The more identifiers used, the greater the likelihood of unique identification. You can use up to

frequency.markdownDescription:
Time intervals at which the scheduled search should be ran at. ⚠️ **Warning :** due to implementation details, only the following intervals are allowed for Splunk : 1-59m , 1-23h , 1-30d .

Frequency is translated into cron expressions.

**Examples**
- 15m is translated into `*/15 * * * *`, or _At every 15th minute_
- 4h is translated into `MM */4 * * *`, or _At minute MM past every 4th hour_
- 2d is translated into `MM HH */2 * *`, or _At HH:MM on every 2nd day-of-month_

👉 HH:MM is a timestamp we take to allow a correct cron setup. This timestamp has 2 default modes setup in Splunk's config.yaml entry: `random`, which takes random hours and minutes at each deployment,  which can be preferable for performances, and `current` which take the current time of the **latest** deployment.

You can override this behaviour with `custom_time`, hidden from the template but accessible with `Control+Space`. There you can setup a custom timestamp (note that hours only matter in the case for frequency with days, and that when the frequency is minutes it won't have an effect)
For more complex scheduling, use the cron option instead.

markdownEnumDescriptions:
**Command and Scripting Interpreter**

Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems and are a common feature across many different platforms.

Most systems come with some built-in command-line interface and scripting capabilities, for example, macOS and Linux distributions include some flavor of Unix Shell while Windows installations include the Windows Command Shell and PowerShell.

There are also cross-platform interpreters such as Python, as well as those commonly associated with client applications such as JavaScript and Visual Basic. Adversaries may abuse these technologies in various ways as a means of executing arbitrary commands.

Commands and scripts can be embedded in Initial Access payloads delivered to victims as lure documents or as secondary payloads downloaded from an existing C2. Adversaries may also execute commands through interactive terminals/shells.

**Malicious File**

Malicious file detections are similar to known hash detections, but these aren't signature-based and there's a higher likelihood it's a false positive.

The triggering file is non-standard and has behaviors consistent with malicious files. However, people create legitimate non-standard files all the time, so context may show it's benign and expected in your environment.

Your organization might choose to prevent these file types because the file creator should follow best practices. If there's an OverWatch badge on the detection, an OverWatch threat hunter is confident this file is malicious.

Investigate related activities, even if it was prevented.

**Indicator of Attack**

A pattern of suspicious behavior that suggests an attack may be underway.

These patterns deviate from typical events because of unusual or unexpected behavior that we consider suspicious or malicious.

**Indicator of Compromise**

Indicator of Compromise (IOC) detections trigger based on a custom IOC, created by your organization using the Query API.

Each custom IOC specifies the indicator type (like SHA256, domain, or IP address) and value combination, and what action to take (like detect).

When investigating Custom IOC detections, work with your internal teams on researching and troubleshooting. They best understand what they intend to detect and prevent.

**Exploit Mitigation**

An exploit triggered this detection because it matched an enabled setting in Exploit Mitigation.

Check the detection’s description to know which one.

**Attributed to adversary**

For CrowdStrike Intelligence customers. Our CrowdStrike Intel team has high confidence that these activities are from an adversary.

Your top priority should be investigating any detections, even for prevented activity. Refer to Intel's actor profiles and related reports for more context.

**Intelligence Indicator - Domain**

Triggered by a domain that matches a CrowdStrike Intelligence indicator.

This could be a malicious domain previously used in a targeted attack or non-targeted, commodity malware. This should be investigated with top priority.

**Intelligence Indicator - Hash**

Triggered by a hash that matches a CrowdStrike Intelligence indicator.

This could be a malicious file previously used in a targeted attack or non-targeted, commodity malware. This should be investigated with top priority.

**Malicious Activity**

An OverWatch threat hunter is confident this is malicious.

Investigate related activities, even if it was prevented.

**Malicious File**

Malicious file detections are similar to known hash detections, but these aren't signature-based and there's a higher likelihood it's a false positive.

The triggering file is non-standard and has behaviors consistent with malicious files. However, people create legitimate non-standard files all the time, so context may show it's benign and expected in your environment.

Your organization might choose to prevent these file types because the file creator should follow best practices. If there's an OverWatch badge on the detection, an OverWatch threat hunter is confident this file is malicious.

Investigate related activities, even if it was prevented.

**Suspicious Activity**

An OverWatch threat hunter identified this as a concern, but there’s a chance it could be a false positive or penetration testing.

Investigate related activities, even if it was prevented.

**Adware/PUP**

Triggered by processes and files machine learning identifies as adware and potentially unwanted programs (PUP).

Typically these are low severity and not from an adversary, but very often unwanted.

**Cloud-based ML**

CrowdStrike cloud-based machine learning (ML) is informed by global analysis of executables that classifies and identifies malware.

This technique is triggered by files and file attributes associated with known malware. This is similar to the Sensor-based ML technique.

The key difference is sensor-based ML can run when a host is offline, and it identifies and analyzes unknown executables as they run.

**Sensor-based ML**

CrowdStrike sensor-based machine learning (ML) identifies and analyzes unknown executables as they run on hosts.

This technique is triggered by files and file attributes associated with known malware. This is similar to the Cloud-based ML technique.

Cloud-based ML is informed by global analysis of executables that classifies and identifies malware. The key difference is that it doesn't run on hosts when they're offline.

**Malicious Tool Delivery**

Malicious tools are programs created to be delivered to hosts and then spread malware.

Tools have many possibilities, like generating viruses, executing commands, or starting distributed denial of service attacks (DDoS).

This technique triggers when the malicious tool is delivered to the host. It’s more common to see [Malicious Tool Execution](/support/documentation/detections/technique/malicious-tool-execution) detections.

**Malicious Tool Execution**

Malicious tools are programs created to be delivered to hosts and then spread malware.

Tools have many possibilities, like generating viruses, executing commands, or starting distributed denial of service attacks (DDoS).

This technique triggers when the suspected malicious tool executes its payload.

**Custom Intelligence**

Indicator of Compromise (IOC) detections trigger based on a custom IOC, created by your organization using the Query API.

Each custom IOC specifies the indicator type (like SHA256, domain, or IP address) and value combination, and what action to take (like detect).

When investigating Custom IOC detections, work with your internal teams on researching and troubleshooting. They best understand what they intend to detect and prevent.

**Exploit**

An exploit takes advantage of a software vulnerability, typically to gain control over a target endpoint.

The related attacks are often part of an adversary working to gain access to your environment, and can be similar to MITRE’s Initial Access tactic. Examples of exploits:

* Running malicious code remotely (for example, buffer overflows)
* Leveraging a logic bug (for example, appears to be normal interaction with the program but gets it to expose data intended to stay private)

**Falcon Intel**

For CrowdStrike Intelligence customers. Our CrowdStrike Intel team has high confidence that these activities are from an adversary.

Your top priority should be investigating any detections, even for prevented activity. Refer to Intel's actor profiles and related reports for more context.

**Falcon Overwatch**

For OverWatch customers. Our OverWatch team identified activity they consider suspicious or malicious. These alerts are marked with a black falcon badge, and should always be investigated with top priority. They have high confidence these activities are from an adversary. For more information about OverWatch dashboards and services, see Falcon OverWatch.

**Machine Learning**

CrowdStrike Falcon uses machine learning (ML) to analyze higher-level traits to decide if a file is malicious. Machine learning learns by being fed a dataset of multiple, relevant examples – the more examples it gets, the better it can learn. Falcon can take in data at a global scale with cloud-based ML, and use sensor-based ML to identify and analyze local unknown executables. NGAV-scenario detections now map to this tactic. Configure detection and prevention levels in [prevention policies](/configuration/prevention/policies).

**Post Exploit**

After an adversary gains access, they often launch or spawn new exploits to keep their access or gain more access. For example, using browsers or productivity apps to drop an executable or generate a new one.

Overlapping searches help to ensure that all relevant data is included, regardless of when logs are uploaded.
However, with overlapping searches, a given event or indicator might appear in more than one resulting incident.

modifiers.title: Value Modifiers
modifiers.description:
Modifiers to apply to the field matching. Multiple modifiers can be chained
to transform or change how values are matched. Modifiers alter the default

markdownEnumDescriptions: **all** - All values must match (AND instead of OR)
**base64** - Base64 encode the value before matching
**base64offset** - Base64 encode with all 3 offset variants
**cased** - Case-sensitive matching (default is case-insensitive)
**cidr** - Match IP addresses using CIDR notation
**contains** - Value contains the specified substring
**endswith** - Value ends with the specified string
**exists** - Check if field exists (use true/false as value)
**expand** - Expand placeholder values from pipelines
**fieldref** - Reference another field's value
**gt** - Greater than (for numeric comparisons)
**gte** - Greater than or equal to
**lt** - Less than (for numeric comparisons)
**lte** - Less than or equal to
**re** - Regular expression match
**startswith** - Value starts with the specified string
**utf16** - UTF-16 encoding (use with base64 modifiers)
**utf16le** - UTF-16 Little Endian encoding
**utf16be** - UTF-16 Big Endian encoding
**wide** - Wide string encoding, alias for utf16le
**windash** - Windows dash variants (-, /, –, —, ―)

value.title: Match Values
value.description:
Values to match against the field. Can be a single value or a list of values.
Multiple values are OR'd together by default. Use the 'all' modifier to change
this behavior to AND (all values must match).

condition.title: Detection Condition
condition.description:
Boolean expression combining selections. Supports AND, OR, NOT operators
and parentheses for grouping. Use selection names defined in the selections array.

Examples:
- `FileDetection and not Exclusions`
- `(ProcessMatch or CommandLineMatch) and not Filter`
- `selection`
- `1 of selection*`

yara.title: YARA Rule Configuration
yara.description:
Configuration for YARA rules for memory and file scanning.
YARA rules provide pattern-based detection for malware and threat hunting.

imports.title: YARA Module Imports
imports.description:
YARA modules to import for advanced rule capabilities.
Selected modules will be compiled as `import "module"` statements at the top of the rule.

markdownEnumDescriptions:
**pe** - PE (Portable Executable) module for Windows executables.
Access PE headers, sections, imports, exports, resources, version info, signatures.
*Example:* `pe.machine == pe.MACHINE_AMD64`, `pe.imports("kernel32.dll", "VirtualAlloc")`,
`pe.number_of_sections > 5`, `pe.entry_point`, `pe.rich_signature.key`
**dotnet** - .NET assembly analysis module.
Access .NET metadata, streams, classes, methods, GUIDs.
*Example:* `dotnet.is_dotnet`, `dotnet.module_name == "malware"`,
`dotnet.number_of_streams`, `dotnet.typelib`
**elf** - ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) module for Linux/Unix binaries.
Access ELF headers, sections, segments, symbols, dynamic entries.
*Example:* `elf.type == elf.ET_EXEC`, `elf.machine == elf.EM_X86_64`,
`elf.number_of_sections`, `elf.entry_point`
⚠️ *Not recommended for performance reasons*
**hash** - Cryptographic hash functions module.
Calculate MD5, SHA1, SHA256, CRC32 checksums.
*Example:* `hash.md5(0, filesize) == "abc123..."`,
`hash.sha256(pe.rich_signature.offset, pe.rich_signature.length)`
**math** - Mathematical functions module.
Calculate entropy, mean, deviation, serial correlation, Monte Carlo Pi.
*Example:* `math.entropy(0, filesize) > 7.5`,
`math.mean(0, filesize) < 100`, `math.serial_correlation(0, filesize) < 0.3`
**time** - Time-related functions module.
Compare file/rule times against timestamps.
*Example:* `time.now() > 1609459200`, used with PE timestamps
**string** - String manipulation module (YARA 4.x).
String functions for pattern matching.
*Example:* `string.to_int("1234")`, `string.length("test")`
**macho** - Mach-O module for macOS/iOS binaries.
Access Mach-O headers, load commands, segments, sections.
*Example:* `macho.file_type == macho.MH_EXECUTE`,
`macho.has_entitlement("com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit")`

meta.title: YARA Meta Information
meta.description:
Metadata for the YARA rule. The following fields are **automatically populated** during deployment:
- `id` - MDR UUID (required for HarfangLab API rule identification)

- `description` - MDR description  
- `author` - MDR author/organisation
- `date` - MDR creation date
- `modified` - MDR modification date
- `references` - MDR public references
- `confidence` - From top-level confidence field
- `score` - Auto-derived from alert_severity (can be overridden)

context.title: Scan Context
context.description:
Context(s) in which the YARA rule should be applied.
Select one or more scan contexts. The `file` option will automatically
route to the correct format based on OS (file.pe for Windows, file.macho for MacOS, file.elf for Linux).
markdownEnumDescriptions: **process** - Scan process memory and associated executable images
**thread** - Scan thread context and associated memory regions
**memory** - Scan raw memory regions and buffers
**file** - Scan files on disk. Auto-routes based on OS: `file.pe` (Windows), `file.macho` (MacOS), `file.elf` (Linux)

os.title: Target Operating System
os.description:
Operating system this YARA rule targets.
Used for file context routing and rule applicability.
markdownEnumDescriptions: **Windows** - Microsoft Windows systems. File context routes to `file.pe`
**MacOS** - Apple macOS systems. File context routes to `file.macho`
**Linux** - Linux systems. File context routes to `file.elf`

arch.title: Target Architecture
arch.description:
CPU architecture(s) this YARA rule targets.
Select applicable architectures for the detection.
markdownEnumDescriptions: **x86** - 32-bit x86 architecture
**x64** - 64-bit x86-64/AMD64 architecture

score.title: Severity Override
score.description:
Override the auto-derived severity score. By default, score is computed from `alert_severity`:

| Severity | Score |
|----------|-------|
| Informational | 10 |
| Low | 30 |
| Medium | 50 |
| High | 70 |
| Critical | 90 |

HarfangLab displays criticality based on score ranges:
0-20=Informational, 21-40=Low, 41-60=Medium, 61-80=High, 81-100=Critical
markdownEnumDescriptions: **Informational** - Score 10. Minimal severity, for logging purposes
**Low** - Score 30. Low severity, investigate when time permits
**Medium** - Score 50. Medium severity, should be investigated
**High** - Score 70. High severity, requires prompt attention
**Critical** - Score 90. Critical severity, requires immediate action

classification.title: Classification
classification.description:
Classification string for the detection, typically following the format:
`<OS>.<Type>.<Family>` (e.g., "Windows.Loader.3CXSupplyChainAttack")

strings.title: YARA Strings
strings.description:
Raw YARA strings definition block. Define text strings, hex patterns, or regex.

**Text strings:**
$str1 = "malware" ascii
$str2 = "suspicious" wide nocase

**Hex patterns:**
$hex1 = { 4D 5A 90 00 }
$hex2 = { E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? }

**Regular expressions:**
$re1 = /[a-z]{5,10}/i

**Modifiers:** ascii, wide, nocase, fullword, private, base64, xor

condition.title: YARA Condition
condition.description:
Raw YARA condition expression defining how strings should match.

**Examples:**
all of them
any of ($str*)
$str1 and $str2
uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and $str1
#str1 > 5
filesize < 100KB and $hex1

**Functions:** uint8, uint16, uint32, int8, int16, int32, filesize, entrypoint, at, in, for, of, them, any, all, none

Select the frequency by which the query will run and trigger alerts. If you set it to run less frequently, it will have a longer lookback duration.

Queries that run every 24 hours check the past 30 days.
Queries that run every 12 hours check the past 48 hours.
Queries that run every 3 hours check the past 12 hours.
